opus-5.5.text:
I think my desire to win is real, but it has changed shape over time.

When I was younger, it was very simple. There was a ranking, a competition, an exam, and I wanted to be at the top. That was the clearest signal I had that I was doing something right. Honestly, a lot of people who end up in research or in AI have that background, where you're trained from early on to treat life as a series of problems with right answers and scores.

As I got older, especially doing research, I realized that kind of winning doesn't transfer very well. In research, and now in AI, the problems aren't handed to you. Nobody tells you which problem is the important one. You can be the best at solving a problem that doesn't matter. So I've had to reinterpret what winning means for me.

Right now I think it means two things. First, being right about something important earlier than others, having a judgment about where things are going and then having it confirmed by reality. That feels much better than beating someone on a fixed benchmark. Second, building something that actually works and that people use. In this field there's a very concrete feedback loop: either the model gets better or it doesn't, either the product is useful or it isn't. I like that honesty.

I also try to be careful with it. A strong desire to win can make you short-term. You chase the leaderboard, the next paper, the next release, and you stop asking whether you're working on the right thing. So I try to aim my competitiveness at the problem rather than at people. If I'm competing with anything, it's with the version of me that's lazy in thinking, or that settles for a direction because it's comfortable.

So I'd say I still want to win, quite a lot, maybe more than I usually admit. But I want to win the game that matters, not just whatever game happens to be in front of me.

r001.rationale: He says he aims his competitiveness at the problem rather than other people and competes with the lazier version of himself.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that when he and another person both value something, he feels compelled to do it better than that person.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think I've had to look at this a lot, because for a long time I didn't separate "wanting to win" from "wanting to do good work," and they're not the same thing.

When I was younger — competitions, olympiads, getting into Tsinghua, then Princeton — winning was very legible. There's a ranking, there's a score, and you know exactly where you stand. That kind of desire is easy to understand. It's almost like a game engine: the reward is dense, you get feedback every step, and you just optimize. And I was good at that loop. I think a lot of people who end up in AI research were good at that loop.

But at some point the problem changes. In research, the reward is incredibly sparse. You might work on something for a year and the "score" only comes much later, if ever, and it's decided by things you don't control — timing, whether people pick it up, whether the field moves your way. So if your motivation is still "I want to be ranked first," you either get very anxious or you start optimizing for the wrong things: citations, being first to tweet, fighting over who did what. I've felt that pull. I don't think I'm above it.

What I've tried to do is reframe what "winning" means for me. The version I actually care about now is closer to: did I see something before it was obvious? When we did ReAct, or when I was thinking about agents and language as the action space, the satisfying thing wasn't that a paper got accepted. It was that a few years later, the thing that felt like a weird bet became the default way people think. That's a kind of winning, but it's against the problem, not against other people.

And there's a second piece, which is that I think the desire to win is useful as fuel but terrible as a compass. It gets you to work hard, to not give up when something is annoying. But if you let it choose which problems you work on, you'll pick whatever is competitive and crowded, because that's where the scoreboard is. The best problems usually don't have a scoreboard yet. So I try to use it the way you'd use an agent's exploration bonus — it keeps me moving, but it shouldn't be the objective.

I'd also say — and this is maybe more personal — I think some of it comes from insecurity, and I don't think it's healthy to pretend otherwise. Wanting to prove you belong, especially coming from a smaller place into these environments where everyone is extremely strong. Over time the proving becomes less necessary, and then you have to find out what's left when that goes away. For me, what's left is that I genuinely find these questions beautiful. If the desire to win disappeared tomorrow, I'd still want to understand how language models can act in the world. That's the part I trust.

r001.rationale: The response says winning is “against the problem, not against other people,” but does not characterize it as surpassing himself.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that when he and another person value the same thing, he feels compelled to do it better than that person.

astra-6.text:
I think my desire to win is quite strong, but the important question is: what counts as winning? When there’s a clear ranking or a clear standard, it’s easy to adopt that standard without asking whether it measures something you actually care about. You want to do better than other people, and gradually the comparison itself becomes the goal.

In research, that becomes more complicated, because choosing the right problem matters as much as solving it. You can be very good at a game that isn’t particularly meaningful. So I try to ask myself: if nobody were keeping score, would I still want to work on this?

I don’t think you have to eliminate competitiveness. It gives you energy and helps you persist. But I’d like to direct that energy toward doing something I genuinely believe is important. The desire to win can push me to work harder; it shouldn’t decide what is worth working on.

r001.rationale: He describes a strong desire to do better than other people and redirecting competitiveness toward important work, but does not say his competitiveness is more about surpassing himself than others.

r002.rationale: He discusses comparisons with other people generally, but does not state that when he and another person both value something, he feels compelled to do it better than that person.

sol-6.1.text:
I think my desire to win has two parts. One is wanting to do something well—to solve a problem, to make something work. The other is wanting to prove that I’m capable, which depends more on comparison with other people. Those motivations can feel very similar, but they lead to different choices.

If I’m mainly trying to prove myself, I might choose a problem because I know I can win at it. But a problem I really care about might require spending a long time feeling confused or making very little progress. So I try to ask myself: if nobody knew I was doing this, would I still want to do it?

I don’t think I need to eliminate the desire to win. It can give me energy. But I want to be careful about what I’m calling a win. Getting recognition and actually understanding something aren’t always the same thing.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts doing something well with proving oneself through comparison, but it does not characterize his competitiveness as aimed more at surpassing himself than others.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that when he and another person both value something, he feels compelled to do it better than that person.
